questions.title: Chemical group uniting the pyrrole rings of a porphyrin
questions.question: The 4 pyrrole rings in porphyrin are united together by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A methyl group (-CH3) is a substituent found on the porphyrin ring's side chains, not the bridge joining the pyrrole rings together.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Methenyl is a similarly named but distinct chemical group; it is not the bridge that unites the pyrrole rings in a porphyrin.
explanations.C: Correct. The four pyrrole rings of a porphyrin are joined into a larger ring by four methylene (=CH-) bridges connecting the alpha-carbons of adjacent pyrrole rings. This tetrapyrrole ring, with its central nitrogen atoms able to chelate a metal ion, is the structural scaffold that becomes haem once ferrous iron is inserted by ferrochelatase at protoporphyrin IX, the final step of haem synthesis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Methanol is a simple alcohol, unrelated to the covalent bridges of the porphyrin ring structure.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Methylene group is a correct, listed answer, so "none of the above" is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: Identify methylene groups as the bridge joining the four pyrrole rings of a porphyrin.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.140

questions.title: Disease from oxidation of iron in hemoglobin
questions.question: If iron in hemoglobin is oxidized, what disease may occur?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cystic fibrosis is a chloride-channel (CFTR) genetic disease unrelated to haemoglobin iron chemistry.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Sickle cell anaemia results from a structural globin-chain amino acid substitution, not from oxidation of the haem iron.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Carbon monoxide poisoning is a competitive-binding condition at the still-ferrous iron of haem — CO does not oxidise the iron, it occupies the same binding site oxygen would use, with higher affinity than O2.
explanations.D: Correct. Oxidation of haemoglobin's iron from the ferrous (Fe2+) to the ferric (Fe3+) state produces methemoglobin, which cannot bind oxygen at all — unlike normal oxyhaemoglobin's reversible, non-oxidative binding of O2 to ferrous iron. A build-up of methemoglobin (methemoglobinemia) reduces the blood's effective oxygen-carrying capacity even though total haemoglobin and iron content are unchanged, and is treated with methylene blue, which reduces the iron back to the ferrous state.
explanations.E: Incorrect. "Haem-haem interaction" describes the cooperative binding behaviour between the four haem groups of haemoglobin, not a disease from iron oxidation.

questions.learning_objective: Identify methemoglobinemia as the condition produced by oxidation of haemoglobin's iron from the ferrous to ferric state.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, Physiology Important MCQ p.110

questions.title: Oxygen binding site of hemoglobin
questions.question: Which of the following is the oxygen binding site of the hemoglobin?

options.B: Carboxyl terminal of both alpha and beta subunits
options.C: Ferric ion (Fe+3) of the heme molecule
options.D: Ferrous ion (Fe+2) of the heme molecule
options.E: Histidine residue of the globin chain

explanations.A: Incorrect. The N-terminal of the beta subunit is involved in 2,3-BPG binding, which modulates oxygen affinity, but it is not the actual oxygen-binding site itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The carboxyl termini of the globin chains participate in the allosteric transitions between the taut and relaxed states of haemoglobin, not in oxygen binding directly.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ferric (Fe3+) iron is the oxidised state found in methemoglobin, which cannot bind oxygen at all — the opposite of a functional binding site.
explanations.D: Correct. The ferrous (Fe2+) iron atom held at the centre of each haem group's porphyrin ring is haemoglobin's actual oxygen-binding site. Oxygen binds reversibly and without oxidising this ferrous iron, which is what allows haemoglobin to load oxygen in the lungs and release it in the tissues repeatedly across its 120-day lifespan.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A histidine residue of the globin chain (the proximal histidine) coordinates and anchors the haem group's iron within the pocket, but the oxygen itself binds directly to the ferrous iron, not to the histidine.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the ferrous (Fe2+) iron of haem as haemoglobin's actual oxygen-binding site.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.143

questions.title: Protein classification of hemoglobin
questions.question: Hemoglobin is a:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A simple protein is composed only of amino acids; haemoglobin's globin portion alone would qualify, but the whole molecule also carries a non-protein haem group, disqualifying "simple" as the classification for haemoglobin overall.
explanations.B: Correct. Haemoglobin is a conjugated protein — its globin portion is a simple protein (four polypeptide chains), but each chain is combined with a haem prosthetic group, a non-protein, iron-containing porphyrin essential to the molecule's oxygen-carrying function. Neither the globin chains alone nor the haem groups alone constitute functional haemoglobin.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A derived protein is a product of protein degradation or denaturation, not an intact functional molecule like haemoglobin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A lipoprotein combines protein with lipid, not with a haem prosthetic group; haemoglobin carries no lipid component.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A nucleoprotein combines protein with nucleic acid, unrelated to haemoglobin's actual haem-globin composition.

questions.learning_objective: Classify hemoglobin as a conjugated protein (globin plus haem prosthetic group).

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.143

questions.title: Jaundice type with both conjugated and unconjugated bilirubin elevated
questions.question: Which type of jaundice is associated with elevation of both conjugated and unconjugated forms of bilirubin?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Haemolytic jaundice, from excess red cell breakdown, raises unconjugated bilirubin predominantly, not both fractions together.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Obstructive jaundice, from blocked bile flow, raises conjugated (direct) bilirubin predominantly, not both fractions together.
explanations.C: Correct. Hepatocellular jaundice, from damaged liver cells (as in hepatitis), impairs uptake, conjugation and excretion of bilirubin all at once, because the liver cell itself is responsible for each of those three functions. This impairs everything together, elevating both conjugated and unconjugated bilirubin — a mixed pattern that distinguishes it from the single-fraction-predominant patterns of haemolytic and obstructive jaundice.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Physiological jaundice of the neonate is from transient unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (immature glucuronyl transferase activity), predominantly unconjugated, not a mixed pattern.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Dubin-Johnson syndrome is a hereditary defect in conjugated bilirubin excretion, predominantly raising conjugated bilirubin, not both fractions together.

questions.learning_objective: Identify hepatocellular jaundice as the pattern that elevates both conjugated and unconjugated bilirubin together.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.142
